A council or emergency-planning officer has to say, in one sentence, whether
hot weather is becoming more frequent. `melbheat` answers that for Melbourne
Airport in three steps, and this article walks through them:

1. count the days each year above a temperature you choose;
2. compare an earlier period with a later one, and say how sure we can be;
3. check whether the answer depends on what you count as "hot".

By the end you will be able to reproduce every number in the app with a
few lines of code, and know how to read it and where it stops being reliable.

## Install and launch

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("ETC5523-2026/etc5523-assignment-4-tngu0386-oss")
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
library(melbheat)
run_app()
```

`run_app()` opens the Shiny app in your browser. The rest of this article uses the same functions the app calls, so
you can work in code or in the app and get identical results.

## The data

`melb_temp` has one row per calendar day, from 1 January 1970 to 26 July 2022,
at the Bureau of Meteorology station 086282 (Melbourne Airport). Days with no
usable reading are kept as `NA` instead of being dropped, so that a gap is
visible rather than silent.

```{r}
library(melbheat)
melb_temp[melb_temp$date >= "2019-01-24" & melb_temp$date <= "2019-01-26", ]
```

| Field | Meaning |
|:--|:----------------------------------------------|
| `date`, `year`, `month` | Calendar date and its year and month |
| `tmax`, `tmin` | Daily maximum and minimum temperature (°C) |
| `tmax_quality`, `tmin_quality` | The Bureau's quality flag for each reading |

The raw files and the script that builds `melb_temp` are in `data-raw/` in the
source repository, so the preparation can be re-run from scratch.

## Step 1: count hot days each year

`annual_exceedances()` counts the days in each year with a daily maximum above a
threshold. The threshold has no default on purpose: what counts as hot is your
decision, and the function asks for it.

```{r}
ex <- annual_exceedances(threshold = 35)
tail(ex, 4)
```

Look at the last row. 2022 has data for only `r ex$n_observed[ex$year == 2022]`
of `r ex$n_days[ex$year == 2022]` days, because the record stops in July, so
`reliable` is `FALSE`. A year is only trusted when at least 80% of its days
were observed (change this with `min_coverage`). Without that rule a short
year would look like a cool one.

`plot_exceedances()` draws the counts. Add `split_year` to see the two periods
being compared.

```{r first-chart}
plot_exceedances(ex, split_year = 2000)
```

The title is the finding, the hottest year is the only bar that is labelled,
and grey bars are the years left out of the averages.

## Step 2: compare two periods and say how sure we are

`summarise_periods()` averages the reliable years either side of a year you
choose, and `describe_periods()` turns the table into sentences.

```{r}
periods <- summarise_periods(ex, split_year = 2000)
periods[, c("period", "n_years", "mean_exceed", "sd_exceed")]
```

```{r}
said <- describe_periods(periods, variable = "tmax", threshold = 35)
said$headline
said$how_sure
```

The "rough 95% range" is the gap between the two averages plus or minus two
standard errors. It treats each year as independent, which neighbouring hot
years are not quite, so read it as a guide to whether the gap is bigger than
ordinary year-to-year variation, not as a formal test.

When there is nothing to compare, the function says so instead of reporting
a gap of zero. Here, a very high threshold in a single month leaves no hot
days at all:

```{r}
rare <- annual_exceedances(threshold = 42, months = 7)
describe_periods(summarise_periods(rare, split_year = 2000),
                 variable = "tmax", threshold = 42)$headline
```

## Step 3: does the answer depend on the threshold?

A conclusion that only holds at 35 °C would be fragile.
`threshold_sensitivity()` repeats the comparison across a range of thresholds.

```{r}
sens <- threshold_sensitivity(thresholds = c(30, 33, 35, 38, 40))
sens[, c("threshold", "mean_before", "mean_after", "difference")]
```

```{r sensitivity-chart}
plot_sensitivity(threshold_sensitivity(), highlight = 35)
```

The later period is higher at every threshold. The gap in days is bigger at
low thresholds simply because there are more such days. The `ratio` column
puts the thresholds on a common footing: later years had roughly 1.2 to 1.5
times as many hot days at most thresholds, and a larger multiple for the
rarest days, where the counts are small and noisier.

### Hot nights

The same functions work for the daily minimum. A hot night is often defined
as a minimum above 20 °C.

```{r hot-nights}
nights <- annual_exceedances(variable = "tmin", threshold = 20)
plot_exceedances(nights, split_year = 2000)
```

## Use the app

Everything above is in the app, with the arithmetic hidden behind controls.

| Control | What it does |
|:------|:--------------------------------------------|
| What are you counting? | Hot days (daily maximum) or hot nights (daily minimum) |
| A day counts if it is above | The threshold, in °C |
| Months to include | Restrict to a season, for example December to February |
| Compare years up to ... with years after | The year that splits the two periods |
| Minimum share of days observed | Under "Show advanced setting"; how complete a year must be to be used |

The **See the trend** tab shows the finding first ("What this shows" and "How
sure are we?"), then the chart, then the period table. **Does the threshold
matter?** is Step 3. **Guide** explains each field. Chart and table can be
downloaded. If your choices leave nothing to count, for example no months
ticked, the app tells you what to change instead of showing an empty chart.

## What this can and cannot tell you

* It is **one weather station**. Other parts of Melbourne can differ.
* Readings are **as recorded**. They are not adjusted for changes in
  instruments or surroundings.
* The comparison shows that hot days were **more frequent later**. It does not
  say why.
* The result depends on the split year you choose, so try several.
* The range from `describe_periods()` is a rough guide, not a hypothesis test.
